Auto-summary (auto-generated): high-level review of audit logging and admin activity capture for Redwood Private/Dedicated; discussed retention, export options (S3, syslog, SIEM), field-level capture and PII concerns, KMS/HSM key usage, and SOC2/ISO alignment.

[00:00] Lena Ortiz: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we have about 55 minutes, we wanted to walk through exactly what we capture in audit logs and admin activity, export options, retention, and then leave time for questions, priya you mentioned compliance items in the invite?

[00:18] Priya Kapoor: yeah thanks lena, just to level set, Northstar needs to know what we can get from audit logs for investigative/audit purposes, how long they can be retained, and options for shipping to our SIEM, plus encryption/KMS controls for logs at rest
[00:32] Marcus Chen: sounds good; i'll start with a quick overview of event classes, then we'll dig into exports and key management, and lena will cover compliance artifacts we can share
[01:05] Tom Reynolds: quick note, we run most infra in us-east-1 and have strict data residency requirements for eu accounts, so if there are cross-region copies that's important to call out

[01:30] Marcus Chen: noted, we support regional storage; for hosted accounts logs are stored in the region of the deployment, for Dedicated and Private you control retention and export targets, so you can keep logs on-prem or in your S3 bucket
[02:10] Sara Lim: can you define "admin activity" vs "audit logs"? sometimes vendors use different terms

[02:30] Marcus Chen: yeah, good question - in our terms: admin activity is user- or admin-initiated actions like user creation, role assignment, model version rollouts, and policy changes. Audit logs include admin activity plus system-level events: auth attempts, token issuance, API calls, model inference events (metadata only), and export operations. We do not log full prompt text in standard audit logs unless configured for compliance evals - default is metadata about requests (model ID, request size, user_id, timestamps, error codes).
[03:15] Priya Kapoor: that last part is important - we need assurance that full user-provided content isn't retained in logs by default. what's your default retention and what fields are logged?

[03:38] Marcus Chen: by default, hosted logs retain audit events for 30 days; Dedicated customers can configure retention; Private you manage retention policy. Fields captured by default: timestamp, actor id (user/service principal), IP address, API endpoint, request_id, model id, request size (tokens), response status, error codes, and event type. Sensitive payloads like full prompts are redacted in default audit logs; we can enable longer retention or payload capture under explicit customer config and contract - typically for PII/PHI workloads customers run Private with strict controls.
[04:10] Tom Reynolds: ok and for a security incident investigation we'd need either a longer retention or a live export into our SIEM - what's available?

[04:30] Marcus Chen: we support three export modes: batched exports to customer S3 (daily/hourly), real-time streaming via syslog/webhook (for SIEM), and direct integration connectors (Splunk/Datadog) via agent. Batched S3 export is easiest to ingest, streaming is lower latency but requires syslog endpoint or Kafka bridge on the customer side.
[05:05] Sara Lim: for S3 exports, are logs encrypted with customer-managed keys?

[05:20] Marcus Chen: yes - we offer server-side encryption with Redwood-managed keys by default, or you can provide a customer-managed KMS key (CMK) for dedicated/private deployments. For Private we also support HSM-backed keys if needed.
[05:48] Priya Kapoor: do you have SOC2 controls around key rotation and access to keys? we need key access auditability

[06:05] Lena Ortiz: yes, our SOC 2 and ISO docs cover KMS usage, rotation policies, key access controls and split of duties; we can share the SOC 2 Type II report and KMS section of the runbook - i'll attach those.

[06:30] Tom Reynolds: great. a couple of specific questions: 1) can we filter which events are sent to S3? we'd like to exclude certain telemetry and only keep admin/change events, 2) what's the schema for events?

[06:55] Marcus Chen: 1) yes you can configure event filters on exports - e.g., only admin_activity, auth_failures, and policy_changes. 2) schema is JSON lines with top-level fields: ts, event_type, actor, resource, action, request_id, ip, region, model_id, tokens_in/tokens_out, status_code, extra (map). we'll share the field list but caveat: auto-transcription - sorry - that's the canonical set. note some names vary slightly in older runtime versions
[07:45] Priya Kapoor: will that schema include user email etc or just user id?

[07:55] Marcus Chen: by default it's a user_id (internal) and actor_email is optional and only included if the calling system sends it; we can map your SSO user ids to the actor_id so you can correlate. PII in logs is avoidable with default config.
[08:30] Sara Lim: about retention windows - you said hosted is 30 days default, what's the maximum configurable without export?

[08:42] Marcus Chen: for Hosted API plans default 30 days; we can extend to 90 days for enterprise tiers. Dedicated has configurable retention up to 1 year, and Private customers control retention directly. For compliance like eDiscovery you can export to your cold storage for multi-year retention.
[09:10] Tom Reynolds: are there retention-based costs? if we keep logs in S3 via Redwood export do you charge for storage/ingest after initial export?

[09:25] Lena Ortiz: export to your own S3 - you pay your storage; Redwood charges a small export fee for outgoing pipeline/ingest and might include long-term retention add-on if managed by Redwood. we'll include a retention/pricing matrix in the follow-up
[09:50] Priya Kapoor: regulatory note: we need logs retained for 7 years for certain EU contracts; is that practical?

[10:05] Marcus Chen: yes, long-term storage in your S3 bucket is standard practice; we can ship logs in parquet format daily for cheaper storage and easier query via Athena, and you can apply lifecycle policies for archival to glacier/deep archive
[10:35] Sara Lim: talk about deletion/retention policies - if a user asks for data deletion, are audit logs redacted?

[10:50] Marcus Chen: good question - for GDPR data deletion requests we can redact PII fields from retained logs, but we cannot remove immutable audit entries that are required for security/compliance; we typically redact or pseudonymize identifiers. There is a process: you submit deletion requests and we verified the scope and then apply redaction to exported logs or to log fields as configured
[11:25] Tom Reynolds: can we integrate your audit logs with our SIEM for alerting on suspicious admin activity?

[11:40] Marcus Chen: yes, streaming to your SIEM via syslog/webhook works; for Splunk we have a connector; for Datadog you can push events to their intake; we can define built-in detection rules (e.g., multiple failed logins, unusual role grants) as part of a managed SIEM onboarding
[12:05] Priya Kapoor: curious about retention of admin activity for platform admin users vs end-users - can we partition?

[12:18] Marcus Chen: yes you can set different retention/export policies by actor type or event class. e.g., keep admin activity for 1 year but general inference metadata 30 days. We'll share an example config file

[12:45] Lena Ortiz: quick plug - we also provide an Audit Log Console in Redwood Console for on-demand search (within retention window) and you can run saved queries; these queries can be exported as CSV or JSON
[13:10] Sara Lim: is console access audited too? who viewed logs?

[13:20] Marcus Chen: yes - console access and log views are captured as separate audit events with actor, timestamp, query_hash; we can record the query text but that is sensitive so it's redacted by default in some modes, but available under the stricter Dedicated/Private configs
[13:55] Priya Kapoor: about encryption at rest and in transit - TLS is assumed; what about KMS? we need customer key control

[14:10] Marcus Chen: TLS for transit. For rest: Redwood-managed KMS by default; you can provide AWS KMS CMK for S3 exports or we can integrate your KMS for Dedicated. For Private we can integrate HSM and you manage keys. Access to KMS operations is logged and included in SOC 2 artifacts
[14:40] Tom Reynolds: any support for split-key or dual-control patterns?
[14:50] Marcus Chen: we support HSM-backed keys and key policies that enforce separation of duties; for enterprise we can discuss key escrow/rotation processes
[15:10] Sara Lim: how long do you keep the log index and what are search capabilities? for fast forensic queries we need 90 days of hot search

[15:25] Marcus Chen: by default we keep hot indexes for 30 days on hosted; we can provision extended hot index windows for enterprise/dedicated customers (e.g., 90 days hot with tiered storage thereafter). Hot search is powered by our log indexing layer; queries support timestamp range, actor, event_type, resource, and free text on error messages
[16:00] Priya Kapoor: legal/procurement question - can logs be exported via a signed contractual SLA for retention? we need the chain of custody

[16:15] Lena Ortiz: yes, retention and export commitments are part of Dedicated/Private contracts; we can include contractual SLAs for log exports and include audit reports as evidence. we'll loop in legal on the next step
[16:40] Tom Reynolds: are there costs/time implications to enabling full request body logging (we might need it for forensics sometimes)?

[16:55] Marcus Chen: enabling full request body capture increases storage and privacy overhead; we typically recommend Private deployments when full payload capture is required due to compliance. For Dedicated we can offer configurable capture but with additional controls and cost adjustments. Also, we recommend tokenization/redaction at ingestion to limit PII exposure
[17:30] Sara Lim: do you have pre-built retention templates aligned to SOC2, PCI, HIPAA?

[17:40] Marcus Chen: we have recommended templates: SOC2 baseline (90-day logs), HIPAA (1 year), EU Regulated (multi-year plus residency), but templates are advisory - customers set final retention via policy
[18:05] Priya Kapoor: audit trail needs: user identity mapping from SSO (Okta) to audit logs, dense enough to show who approved changes - can you integrate Okta SAML/SCIM?

[18:22] Marcus Chen: yes we support SSO via SAML, SCIM provisioning, and we ingest the SAML subject/okta uid as actor_id. Provisioning events (user created/assigned) are captured as audit events and can be correlated
[18:55] Tom Reynolds: one more technical question: how do you ensure log integrity? tamper-evidence?

[19:10] Marcus Chen: we support append-only log storage and can sign exports (SHA256 manifests) and provide checksums. For higher assurance we can route logs to an immutable store or use Write-Once-Read-Many (WORM) storage on customer S3
[19:40] Sara Lim: for incident response, can we have a near-real-time stream with sub-minute latency?
[19:55] Marcus Chen: yes with streaming syslog/webhook/Kafka bridge we can get under 1 minute in most cases depending on your collector. We'll test latency during the technical deep-dive
[20:20] Priya Kapoor: let's discuss a concrete example: an admin rolled out a new model and an unintended data leak - what does the audit record look like and how do we investigate?

[20:38] Marcus Chen: the rollout event captures actor, change_type (model_deploy), previous_version, new_version, timestamps, IP, and associated request_ids for recent inferences. If full payload capture was enabled we can correlate recent inference request_ids to stored payloads in exports; if not, you get metadata sufficient to identify affected users and timelines and then we coordinate snapshot exports for forensics
[21:15] Tom Reynolds: forensics require chain of custody - will the export be forensically sound?

[21:25] Marcus Chen: we produce signed export bundles with manifests and checksums; if required we can do an on-demand forensic export and a Redwood SE will guide the process. It's part of our incident response runbook
[22:00] Priya Kapoor: any automation for alerts on policy regression after a rollout?

[22:12] Marcus Chen: yes you can wire alerts from the audit stream into your SIEM; Redwood Optimize also supports quality/regression monitors tied to prompt sets and evals, and we can create a rule to detect sudden spikes in error codes or high token anomaly
[22:50] Sara Lim: let's circle back to data residency - if we need logs to remain in eu-west-1, can Redwood guarantee that?

[23:05] Marcus Chen: yes for Hosted we have region-specific deployments and store logs in the same region. For Dedicated/Private it's controlled by customer network and storage. We can include residency clauses in contracts for enterprise
[23:30] Tom Reynolds: are there any limitations with third-party connectors for streaming? like max throughput or event size?

[23:45] Marcus Chen: connectors have throughput limits based on plan and instance size; large spikes are buffered and we recommend configuring backpressure policies. Event max size is ~256KB per event; larger payloads should be archived to S3 and referenced in the event
[24:20] Priya Kapoor: security controls around who can configure export destinations - RBAC?

[24:30] Marcus Chen: yes - exports and retention policies are RBAC protected. We have roles: admin, security_admin, auditor, and custom roles via RBAC policies. Only security_admin or owner roles can change exports. All changes are themselves logged as audit events
[25:00] Lena Ortiz: quick interjection: we'll include a sample RBAC mapping for your team in our follow-up
[25:10] Sara Lim: do you support multi-tenant audit separation? we have multiple business units and need tenant-level isolation
[25:25] Marcus Chen: yes, logs are partitioned by tenant ID and you can enforce strict access controls per tenant. For Dedicated we can isolate tenants to separate storage buckets if desired
[26:00] Tom Reynolds: compliance artefacts - will you provide regular attestation or logs about who accessed what?
[26:12] Lena Ortiz: Redwood provides periodic compliance artifacts; we can also enable an access review export which lists console logins and file access over a period
[26:40] Priya Kapoor: any known gaps or limitations we should be aware of?

[26:52] Marcus Chen: older runtime versions had slightly different field names and lacked request token counts; if you need uniformity we recommend standardizing on a single runtime version for your Dedicated cluster. Also, by default we do not capture full inference payloads unless configured - that's the main limitation for deep forensics on hosted without special config
[27:20] Tom Reynolds: ok understood. a short note: our legal team will want to see sample export files and the checksums, can you provide those?
[27:32] Lena Ortiz: yes, marcus will prepare a redacted sample export and signed manifest
[27:40] Marcus Chen: noted - i'll include an example parquet export with schema and a manifest
[28:00] Priya Kapoor: SLA expectations - if exports fail do you retry and alert?
[28:15] Marcus Chen: we have retry logic and alerting; failures are logged and we can create an automated Jira or pager alert to your ops if you want guaranteed delivery SLAs in contract
[28:40] Sara Lim: about log deletion - in Private mode if we need to honor a court order or e-discovery hold, can Redwood place a hold?
[28:55] Marcus Chen: for Private/ Dedicated, yes you can set legal holds that prevent lifecycle deletion. For Hosted we can support holds via contract with log export to your bucket and hold there
[29:20] Tom Reynolds: what about access reviews and SSO provisioning sync cadence?
[29:30] Marcus Chen: SCIM provisioning syncs are near real-time; access review exports are run on demand or scheduled (daily/weekly) and we can provide auditors with the CSV

[30:12] Lena Ortiz: we have SOC2 Type II and ISO 27001 certificates; i'll send them and the summary controls mapping, plus a table mapping Redwood controls to Northstar control IDs

[30:45] Marcus Chen: yes keys are masked; logs show key id hash, not the raw key. Credential rotation events are also captured
[31:10] Tom Reynolds: sample timeline for getting Dedicated or Private deployed?

[31:22] Lena Ortiz: Dedicated onboarding typically 4-8 weeks depending on capacity and networking, Private varies (6-12 weeks) depending on on-prem requirements. We'll work with your infra to scope it out
[31:50] Priya Kapoor: any compliance pen tests or third-party attestation?
[32:00] Marcus Chen: we do annual pen tests and a third-party assessor for SOC2; results summary included in SOC pack, and additional pentesting can be arranged under NDA
[32:25] Sara Lim: ok to circle back to the schema - would appreciate a CSV mapping of fields to pii sensitivity and examples
[32:35] Marcus Chen: yes we'll provide a field-by-field mapping and a redaction guide
[33:00] Tom Reynolds: how are admin activity logs correlated with metrics/traces for a combined investigation?

[33:12] Marcus Chen: we emit trace_ids and correlate request_ids to our tracing system, and we can cross-reference that to logs in your export. We also support ingesting application traces to the same SIEM so you can correlate events
[33:45] Priya Kapoor: about retention change requests - is there an API to adjust retention programmatically?
[33:55] Marcus Chen: yes, for Dedicated/Private there's an admin API to change retention/export configs; API calls are themselves logged so you get auditability
[34:20] Sara Lim: if we want immediate push to our S3, what's the typical lag?
[34:30] Marcus Chen: near-real-time push is possible via streaming; batched S3 exports are typically delivered hourly with an end-of-hour manifest, or daily depending on your preference
[34:58] Tom Reynolds: curious about archival format - parquet vs jsonl?
[35:10] Marcus Chen: we support JSONL by default and Parquet for cost-efficient long-term storage; parquet includes typed columns and is better for queries
[35:30] Priya Kapoor: access controls for exported buckets - do you write directly into customer buckets using an assumed role?

[35:40] Marcus Chen: for S3 exports we use cross-account write with a limited IAM role you provision; that ensures we never store your data in our bucket unless contracted. Role creation steps included in the onboarding doc
[36:05] Sara Lim: about deletion again - if you redact logs, do you preserve the event shape so analytics still work?
[36:15] Marcus Chen: yes redaction replaces PII values with stable pseudonyms so you can still run counts and trend analytics while removing sensitive values
[36:40] Lena Ortiz: we're about halfway through timewise, do you want to go deeper into any area?
[36:48] Priya Kapoor: KMS integration and exports to SIEM are top priorities, then a sample export + schema

[37:05] Marcus Chen: ok i'll summarize steps for both: KMS - we'll walk you through creating a CMK and granting Redwood limited decrypt/encrypt permissions, we can log all KMS ops. SIEM - pick streaming or batched; we'll provide connector configs and throughput guidance
[37:35] Tom Reynolds: we also want to onboard a test export to validate schema and checksums before committing to retention policy

[38:20] Marcus Chen: we can pseudonymize actor references after deletion or keep an internal mapping for audit purposes depending on legal needs, documented in the deletion policy
[38:50] Priya Kapoor: we may require HSM-backed key storage for some logs - how does that change the process?
[39:05] Marcus Chen: HSM adds an onboarding step, we coordinate with your security/infra, keys never leave HSM, and key ops are restricted. We'll detail options in the KMS integration doc

[40:30] Marcus Chen: yes thresholds are configurable in your SIEM or in our alerting policies; for managed detection we can jointly tune rules
